title: The Gospel According to Islam
excerpt: A gospel retold with the Qur’an as the measure.

title: How this gospel was composed
excerpt: The rules used to compose the gospel: what is kept, what is left out, and why.

title: Early writings in this gospel
excerpt: Six early Christian writings and their sayings of Jesus, kept or set aside by the measure of the Qur’an.
body: 1 Clement, the Epistle of Barnabas, the Gospel of Mary, the Epistle of the Apostles, Tatian’s Diatessaron and the Didache all quote or retell the speech of Jesus. Their sayings were weighed against the Qur’an one at a time, and the result is in The Gospel According to Islam.
## The rule

A saying is kept when it does not contradict the Qur’an. A saying that does contradict it is left out, and the reason is written down on the page of early writings set aside. The sayings of Thomas were treated the same way, and the colour marks are the same (the Thomas sayings set aside).
Each saying is judged on its own words. A good saying set in a scene the Qur’an does not give is kept without the scene, and the note says so.
## The six writings
- 1 Clement, written from Rome to Corinth about 96 CE. Translation: Roberts and Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers 1. Kept: 2 sayings, both given as “the words of the Lord Jesus”. Set aside: 3 passages.
- The Epistle of Barnabas, written between about 70 and 135 CE. Translation: Roberts and Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers 1. Kept: 3 sayings. Set aside: 1 passage.

- The Gospel of Mary, a second-century work; the Coptic text is in Papyrus Berolinensis 8502. Translation: Mark M. Mattison, public domain, at gospels.net. Kept: 3 sayings. Set aside: 3 passages. Pages 1 to 6 and 11 to 14 are lost.

- The Epistle of the Apostles, which M. R. James, following Carl Schmidt, dates to about 160 CE. Translation: James, The Apocryphal New Testament (1924). Kept: 10 sayings. Set aside: 16 passages, among them its prophecy of Paul.
- Tatian’s Diatessaron, about 170 CE, a harmony of the four gospels. Translation: Hope W. Hogg, Ante-Nicene Fathers 9. Kept: 2 sayings. It adds no saying that the four gospels lack.
- The Didache, a church manual of the late first or early second century. Translation: M. B. Riddle, Ante-Nicene Fathers 7. It is used in footnotes only.
## How the Didache is used

The Didache is cited in the notes and not set among the sayings. Its teaching on enemies, the two commandments and the hour agrees with the Qur’an and is footnoted where a saying of the same kind stands. Its thanksgiving through “Jesus Your Servant” is noted at the mission of the Twelve. Its baptismal formula, which names three, is set aside with the reason.
## What the kept sayings add

Almost every kept saying has a parallel in Matthew, Mark or Luke, so the early writings mostly witness to words already in the gospels. Barnabas 7:11, on reaching Jesus through hardship, is the clearest saying that none of the four gospels carries.

The sayings left out are chiefly of three kinds: sayings that make the passion the speech of Jesus, sayings in which he claims the nature or the powers of God, and sayings that give him judgment, forgiveness or intercession. Each is answered from the Qur’an on the page of sayings set aside.
Anyone who wishes to check a saying can read the source in the translations named above; each is in the public domain.

title: Early writings set aside
excerpt: The sayings of Jesus in six early writings that are not used in this gospel, each with the reason.
body: Each saying of Jesus in six early writings was tested against the Qur’an as the measure (see the measure). 21 are used in The Gospel According to Islam, each with a colour mark and a note. The 26 listed here are not used, and the reason is given for each: 22 conflict with the Qur’an, 3 only repeat what is used elsewhere, and 1 are too uncertain to place.
## The colour marks
- [agree] Agrees with the Qur’an as the measure.
- [beyond] Beyond the measure: the Qur’an says nothing either way. Included, and marked.
- [unclear] Unclear: the words or their sense are uncertain. Included where the words can stand, and marked; here, left out.
- [conflict] Conflicts with the Qur’an: the saying says what the Qur’an denies, or denies what it affirms. Not used.
- [notneeded] Not needed: it repeats a saying that is already used. Not used.
## Scenes and words

A saying is judged on its own words. Where a source sets a good saying in a scene the Qur’an does not give, such as a meeting with Jesus after a crucifixion, the saying is kept and the scene is not, and the note on the saying says so. Where the saying itself carries the claim the Qur’an denies, the whole saying goes. “Father” is read as on the page of Thomas sayings set aside.
## 1 Clement

- [conflict] 1 Clement 16. Clement reads Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22 as the voice of Christ, so that “I am a worm, and no man” is put in the mouth of Jesus at his passion. Makes the passion the subject of Jesus’s own speech. The Qur’an says they did not kill him and did not crucify him (4:157).

- [notneeded] 1 Clement 22:1-8. “Come, ye children, hearken unto me”: Clement says Christ addresses the Corinthians through the Holy Spirit. The words are Psalm 34:11-17, which no gospel gives to Jesus and which the Qur’an gives to no one but God’s earlier messengers (4:163). It adds nothing the chapters need.

- [conflict] 1 Clement 36:4. The Father says to the Son, “Thou art my Son, to-day have I begotten thee” (Psalm 2:7-8). God is not said to beget, and Jesus is not God’s son in the Qur’an (19:35; 112:3-4).
## The Epistle of Barnabas

- [conflict] Barnabas 5 to 6. Barnabas makes Jesus the speaker of Isaiah 50 (“I have given my back to scourges, and my cheeks to blows”) and of Psalm 22 at the passion. Same reason as 1 Clement 16: the scene is the crucifixion, which the Qur’an denies (4:157).
## The Gospel of Mary

- [conflict] Gospel of Mary, page 7. Asked what the sin of the world is, the Savior says that sin does not exist, and that people make it by acting as adulterers do. The Qur’an treats sin as real, and teaches repentance and forgiveness from God (3:135; 4:48; 39:53). A saying that denies sin denies the need to repent.

- [conflict] Gospel of Mary, pages 7 and 8. Every nature and form dissolves into its roots. Matter gave birth to a passion with no image, and the Good came among people to restore each nature to its root. Gives matter the power to bear a passion, and gives the Savior the work of restoring creation. In the Qur’an God creates all things (6:102; 39:62) and the Messiah restores nothing by his own power (5:110).

- [conflict] Gospel of Mary, pages 10 to 17. In Mary’s report of a vision, the mind sees, and the soul climbs past powers called Darkness, Desire, Ignorance and Zeal for Death, the seven powers of Wrath, and leaves them behind. The Qur’an knows no such powers over the soul. The soul meets angels and then judgment (6:61-62; 7:40), and Jesus teaches nothing in secret: he says only what God commanded (5:117). Pages 1 to 6 and 11 to 14 are lost, so some of the teaching cannot be tested at all.
## The Epistle of the Apostles
The translation is that of M. R. James, The Apocryphal New Testament (Oxford, 1924). The Coptic text of the first chapters is lost, and James follows the Ethiopic there.

- [notneeded] Epistle of the Apostles 5. Jesus asks who touched him, tells the woman her faith has made her whole, rebukes Legion, and sends a disciple to find a coin in a fish. Each word repeats a saying in Mark 5 or Matthew 17:27. The disciples’ reading of the five loaves as faith in “the Father, Jesus Christ, the Holy Ghost” is theirs, not his, and conflicts with 4:171 and 5:73.

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 10 to 12. Jesus appears to the women at the tomb, bids Peter put a finger in the nail print and Thomas in the wound in his side, and tells Andrew to look at his feet. The risen, crucified body is what 4:157 denies: they did not kill him and did not crucify him. God raised him to Himself (4:158).

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 13. Jesus came down from the Father through the heavens, took the likeness of the angels so that the archangels followed him unrecognised, and became “all things in all”. The Qur’an has Jesus created, like Adam, by God’s word “Be” (3:59), and the angels serve God and are never deceived about their Lord (21:26-28; 4:172).

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 14. Jesus says that he took the form of the angel Gabriel, appeared to Mary, and “formed myself and entered into her body”, being his own messenger. Gabriel is a separate angel sent by God to Maryam (19:17-21; 2:97-98), and God gives the child (19:19-21). No one makes himself.

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 15. The disciples are told to commemorate his death at Passover; one will be freed from prison by his power “in the form of mine angel Gabriel”. Commemorates a death that the Qur’an says did not happen (4:157), and makes Gabriel a form of Jesus (see chapter 14).

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 16 and 47. Jesus will come “like the sun”, with the sign of the cross before him, “to judge the quick and the dead”, and on that day will show no pity to the poor and no regard for the rich. His return before the Hour is in the Qur’an (43:61; 4:159), and the sun and the cross do not matter to it. The cross is the crucifixion (4:157), and judgment is God’s: He is “Master of the Day of Judgment” (1:4), and Jesus is asked on that day what he told people (5:116-118).

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 17. “I am wholly in the Father and my Father is in me”: he is the Father’s Word, in his likeness and power and fullness and light. Shared nature. The Qur’an calls the Messiah a word from God (3:45; 4:171) and in the same verse tells people not to say “three”, and it denies that the Messiah is God (5:72-73; 112:3-4).

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 19 to 21. He is “wholly at the right hand of the Father”, “unbegotten and yet begotten of mankind, without flesh and yet bearing flesh”, with “the whole power of my Father”, “the resurrection of the dead”. Claims to be unbegotten and yet born, and to hold the power that the Qur’an gives to God (112:3; 3:26). Where the Messiah gives life to the dead, it is by God’s leave (3:49; 5:110).

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 26. The Father says: “My Son, in the day of judgement thou shalt have no respect for the rich, neither pity for the poor”, and gives him authority to do what he wills. God speaks to Jesus as “Son” and hands him the judgment. The Qur’an does neither (19:35; 5:116-118).

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 27 and 28. Jesus went down to the place of Lazarus, preached to the righteous and the prophets, “poured out” baptism and forgiveness on them and on the disciples, and redeemed them from “the rulers”. The descent to the dead is beyond the measure, but the speech joins it to forgiveness and redemption given by Jesus, and to rulers over the soul. In the Qur’an God alone forgives (3:135), and the Messiah is a servant who redeems no one by his own hand (5:17).

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 31 and 33. Jesus foretells a Jew named Saul, called Paul, who will meet the apostles, hear his voice from heaven, be blinded and healed by their hands, and become “the last of the last”, a preacher to the Gentiles. After Jesus goes home to the Father, he “will speak unto him from heaven”. In these words Jesus speaks from heaven to a person on earth and makes the apostles that man’s guides. In the Qur’an Jesus says he was a witness over his people only while he remained among them, and that God was the watcher over them once He took him up (5:117); it gives him no speech to anyone after that. The same passage has him say “I am the word of the Father and the Father is in me” (5:73; 112:3-4). The Epistle itself opens against Simon and Cerinthus as false apostles, and M. R. James reports Carl Schmidt’s date for it: about 160 CE, in Asia Minor, a century after Paul’s death.

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 39 (end). “I am the word: I became flesh”; “the Son of God, which Son am I”; “the Father that hath sent me”. The Qur’an denies the Messiah that title of sonship (9:30-31; 19:35). The words before it, on free choice, are kept.

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 40. Asked whether anyone intercedes for the sinners, Jesus says “Yea, and I will hearken unto the prayer of the righteous which they make for them”. Makes Jesus the one who hears prayer. The Qur’an says no one intercedes except by God’s leave (2:255) and has Jesus disown prayer to himself (5:116).

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 41 and 42. After quoting “Call no man your father upon earth”, Jesus tells the apostles they will be “fathers and servants and masters”, giving “baptism through me” and “the remission of their sins at my hand through you”. Contradicts its own quotation of Matthew 23:9-10, sets up men as lords beside God (9:31), and gives them forgiveness of sins, which belongs to God (3:135).

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 43 to 45. The ten virgins become Faith, Love, Grace, Peace and Hope, and Knowledge, Understanding, Obedience, Patience and Compassion. Jesus says “I am the Lord and I am the bridegroom”, and calls all ten “daughters of God, even the Father”. Turns Matthew 25:1-13 into a claim of lordship and of divine children. The Qur’an rejects the claim to be God’s children (5:18) and the claim that the Messiah is the Lord (5:72).

- [conflict] Epistle of the Apostles 51. “On the third day and at the third hour shall he come which hath sent me, that I may depart with him”, and, on rising, “Depart hence in peace”. Ends the post-crucifixion teaching of chapters 10 to 12, which is not kept. The Qur’an has God raise Jesus to Himself (4:158) and says nothing of a third day or a post-crucifixion farewell.
## The Diatessaron

- [notneeded] Diatessaron, whole work. Tatian arranged the four gospels into one continuous story, so every saying of Jesus in it is already in Matthew, Mark, Luke or John. Each is either used elsewhere in this gospel from those four, or set aside there on its own words. The two sayings it carries that bear most on the Qur’an are kept above.
## The Didache

- [conflict] Didache 7:1 and 7:3. Baptise “into the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”, and pour water three times on the head if there is no running water. A baptismal formula that names three. The Qur’an says not to say “three” (4:171; 5:73). The Didache itself says at 9:5 that its people are “baptized into the name of the Lord”, so the longer wording may be a later addition.

- [unclear] Didache 8:2. The Lord’s Prayer, to be said three times a day. The prayer begins “Our Father”. The Qur’an does not address God so, though it does not forbid the word where no sonship is claimed (see the note on “Father”). Prayer three times a day is beyond the measure. Left out of the text for that reason; the Didache is not a saying of Jesus in its own right.
## What the Epistle says about Paul
A reader who holds that Paul was a true apostle will point to chapters 31 and 33 of the Epistle of the Apostles. They are the earliest text in which Jesus himself is made to name Paul.

The reply rests on the Qur’an alone. It gives Jesus no speech to any person after God raised him, and in 5:117 it has Jesus say that he was a witness over his people while he remained among them. That reading of 5:117 is this site’s own, and it is open to question. The passage is therefore set aside, with the reason above, and not hidden. For the wider case, see Paul of Tarsus.
